opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's one where people sometimes expect a more dramatic answer than the one I actually believe.

My general view is that attention and state space models like Mamba are good at different things, and they're complementary rather than strictly competing. You can think of a state space model as having a compressed, fixed-size state. It's constantly summarizing everything it has seen into that state, which makes it very efficient and quite good at processing long, raw, continuous streams of data. Attention is almost the opposite. It keeps a cache of everything and can look back and retrieve precise pieces of information. That's very powerful, but it's expensive, and it works best when the individual tokens are already meaningful units.

So when you have a modality with a well-tuned end-to-end pipeline, like language with a good tokenizer, or vision with a patching scheme people have optimized for years, a lot of the hard work of turning raw data into meaningful chunks has already been done for you. In that setting, attention is a very natural fit, and I wouldn't expect a pure SSM to beat it everywhere. What we've seen empirically, and what I'd recommend in practice, is hybrids: mostly SSM layers with a small fraction of attention layers mixed in. The SSM layers give you efficiency and good general sequence modeling, and the attention layers give you that precise retrieval. Those hybrids tend to match or beat pure Transformers while being much cheaper at inference, especially for long contexts.

Where I think it gets more interesting is when you question the pipeline itself. A lot of these pipelines exist partly because attention needs them. Tokenization is a good example. It's a hand-designed preprocessing step that's there in part because attention over raw bytes or characters is too expensive and not very effective. If you have models that handle raw, high-resolution data better, you can start pushing the learning further down the stack and let the model figure out its own chunking, instead of committing to something fixed ahead of time.

So my short answer is: if the pipeline is already well tuned, don't throw it away. Drop in SSM layers where you want efficiency, keep some attention for retrieval, and you'll probably get a better trade-off. But longer term, I think the bigger win is rethinking those pipelines so the model learns more of the abstraction itself, and that's where I think these architectures have the most to offer.

r001.rationale: For a well-tuned pipeline, it recommends keeping some attention for precise retrieval and says attention is a natural fit; this communicates that attention still has an essential role.

r002.rationale: It recommends hybrids with mostly SSM layers and a small fraction of attention layers.

r003.rationale: It says SSMs are efficient for long, raw streams, while attention works best with meaningful tokens, and suggests learning more directly from raw data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on where the modality sits, and I try not to be dogmatic about it. If you have something like vision or speech where people have spent years tuning a pipeline end to end, the architecture is usually not the bottleneck anymore. The tokenization, the data, the training recipe, all of that has been co-adapted to the model that's there, which is mostly attention. So dropping in a new sequence layer and expecting a free win is kind of naive. You'd be fighting against all those accumulated inductive biases that were tuned around Transformers.

Where I think these state space or Mamba-style models actually earn their place is when the data has a lot of redundancy or it's very long and raw. Audio waveforms, DNA, long video, anything where you haven't already compressed the input into nice discrete tokens. Attention is really good at operating on information-dense tokens where every element matters and you want precise retrieval. Selective state space models are good at compressing a stream of less meaningful units into something more abstract. So the way I'd frame it is: the two mechanisms have different strengths, and the question is less "which one wins" and more "where in the pipeline does each one belong."

In practice that pushes me toward hybrids. You might use a recurrent or SSM-style backbone to do the heavy lifting on long, low-level sequences, and then put a few attention layers on top where you need the in-context retrieval or the exact copying behavior. The empirical results on language seem to point that way too, something like a small fraction of attention layers mixed into a mostly SSM model tends to do better than either one alone.

And the deeper thing I'd say is that if a pipeline is already very well tuned, part of what you're seeing is the tokenizer doing the work the model would otherwise have to do. One of the things I find exciting about these architectures is that they might let you remove some of those hand-engineered stages and let the model learn the compression itself. But that's a bet on end-to-end learning over a longer horizon, not a claim that you can swap a layer tomorrow and see the gains.

r001.rationale: The response describes attention’s strengths and recommends keeping some attention layers for retrieval, but it does not state that attention remains indispensable when a modality already has a well-tuned end-to-end pipeline.

r002.rationale: It says a small fraction of attention layers in a mostly SSM model can outperform either approach alone, clearly making attention a minority component.

r003.rationale: It says Mamba-style models earn their place with long, raw, or uncompressed inputs, while attention suits information-dense tokens.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what that pipeline is already doing well. If you have a really well-tuned system for a modality, I wouldn’t assume that replacing everything with attention or Mamba is going to improve it. The question is where you need information to interact, and what kind of interaction you need.

Attention is useful when you want to look back at particular pieces of the input and retrieve them directly. With Mamba, you’re processing a sequence through a state, so you have a different tradeoff: you can process long sequences efficiently, but you’re asking that state to retain the information you’ll need later.

So I’d think of these as components you can combine with the existing pipeline. You might keep the modality-specific processing and use a sequence model where you need broader context. And that sequence model could itself be a hybrid. I don’t think there’s a requirement that every layer use the same mechanism—the useful question is whether each component improves the overall system at the quality and compute budget you care about.

r001.rationale: The response says attention is useful for retrieving specific input pieces, but does not state that it remains indispensable with a well-tuned pipeline.

r002.rationale: It suggests combining sequence models with modality-specific processing, but does not say attention should make up only a small part of the model.

r003.rationale: It describes attention and Mamba tradeoffs, but does not connect how processed the input is to the importance of using non-attention architectures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to look at what role the architecture is actually playing in that pipeline. Attention is very good at letting you selectively retrieve information from anywhere in a sequence. Mamba has a different tradeoff: you’re compressing the history into a state, which gives you efficient processing as the sequence gets longer, but you don’t have that same explicit access to every previous token.

So if a modality already has a really well-tuned end-to-end pipeline, I wouldn’t assume that replacing everything with attention or replacing everything with Mamba is the right approach. You can ask where you need that selective interaction and where you mostly need to process a long stream efficiently. That might suggest a hybrid, or it might suggest changing only one part of the model.

Ultimately, the comparison has to be at the level of the whole system. Does it improve quality, throughput, memory, or latency under the constraints you actually care about? Being a better sequence modeling layer in isolation doesn’t automatically make it a better fit for that pipeline.

r001.rationale: The response describes attention’s selective retrieval strength and cautions against replacing everything with either architecture, but does not state that attention remains indispensable.

r002.rationale: It suggests changing only one part or using a hybrid, but does not argue that attention should make up only a small part of the model.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect how processed the input data is to the importance of architectures other than attention.
